# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This follow-up responds directly to the open questions from earlier rounds. It adds an hours measure that captures unclaimed work, registers the meetings test in advance, applies like-for-like comparisons, and checks the meta-analysis's duration claim against its supplementary table. That last check confirms the concern I raised. The main problems are:

* Some control offices started cutting meetings partway through, which affects the decay estimate.
* The mediation result is described more strongly than the design allows.
* Several outcomes requested in earlier rounds are still missing.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Calculation | Paper |
|---|---|---|
| Output per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Output per hour, logs | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085 | +8.5% ✓ |
| CI, timesheets (hours fixed) | 0.920–1.012 / 0.88 → +4.5 to +15.0 | +4.6 to +15.2 ✓ |
| CI, logs (hours fixed) | 0.920–1.012 / 0.89 → +3.4 to +13.7 | +3.4 to +13.8 ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100 ✓ |
| Meetings, difference-in-differences | (3.9 − 7.4) − (7.0 − 7.2) | −3.3 h/week, matching the 9-month figure ✓ |
| Halden hours | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 | −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden output per hour | 96.8 / 86.6 = 1.118 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Timesheet decline | 9.8 / 12.5 | −22%, "about a quarter" ✓ |

The paper compares the 9- and 24-month results using timesheets at both points, which is correct. The 12.5% → 8.5% comparison in the Summary mixes two different hours measures.

## Main issues

**1. Control offices cutting meetings may explain part of the apparent decay.**
* From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut standing meetings and gained about 4.1% output per hour.
* That raises the control average by roughly 2/7 × 4.1 ≈ 1.2 points over months 15–24.
* The difference-in-differences shrinks by about that much. That alone could account for nearly half of the fall from 12.5% to 9.8%, without the treated offices fading at all.
* A meeting audit in a control office during a trial run by the same employer is likely a spillover from the trial. Avoiding spillover is the reason the trial randomised by office.
* Needed:
  * a sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or censoring them at month 15;
  * a treated-only trajectory alongside the difference-in-differences.

**2. The control meetings figures look internally inconsistent.**
* If two of seven control offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, the control mean should drop by about 0.6 hours.
* The reported control change is only 7.2 → 7.0. Either the other five offices increased meetings by about 0.4 hours on average, or the figures are weighted or averaged differently.
* This needs explaining, because the size of the meetings mediator depends on it.

**3. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result.**
* **The same offices that generated the hypothesis tested it.** The test was registered at month 11, after the 9-month exploratory finding and with meetings data through month 11 already visible, and it was run on the same seven treated offices. Registering in advance protects against picking the analysis after seeing the result. It doesn't turn this into an independent replication. The re-analysis's specific objection, that such findings don't replicate, still needs new offices to answer it.
* **More office-months add little information.** The randomised unit is the office (14 in total), and months within an office are correlated. A CI of 28–66% for a mediated share with 14 clusters looks narrow. The paper should report how clustering was handled.
* **Mediation itself is not randomised.** Treatment was assigned at random; meeting cuts were not. Managers who cut meetings may differ in ways that also raise output. The Limitations section says this, but the Summary's "confirms" ignores it.
* **Mediator shares can't simply be added.** Fewer meetings plausibly reduce fatigue, so the two mediators are probably related, and splitting the effect into 47% and 18% depends on model assumptions. The paper should report the model specification and whether it tested an interaction.

**4. The decline itself is not tested.**
* The 9- and 24-month CIs overlap heavily, so the confidence interval for the change probably includes zero.
* "The gain has therefore declined" in the Summary should match the body's "consistent with some fading".
* With only two time points, the shape of the trajectory is unknown. That is the same criticism the paper rightly makes of the re-analysis's straight-line extrapolation of the energy data.
* The monthly series exists and should be shown.

**5. The log-hours measure needs definition and a baseline.**
* The paper says the measure was "added" at follow-up. A difference-in-differences figure of −11% needs log data from before the trial. If the system retains historical logs, the paper should say so.
* "Active log-in time on cases" probably excludes meetings and work outside the system. In that case it isn't a superset of timesheet hours, and its role as the outcome denominator in a mediation analysis about meetings needs explaining.
* An 11% fall versus a 12% fall shows a *smaller relative reduction*. It doesn't by itself show "more work than timesheets"; comparing levels would.
* The same applies to baseline meeting hours (7.4 and 7.2). The 9-month report said calendar data were first collected at month six, so the source of the baseline should be stated.

**6. Outcomes requested in earlier rounds are still missing.**
* **Time-to-decision and backlog** for case processing. This was registered at nine months, and the 9-month Limitations specifically raised whether backlogs would breach statutory deadlines. Two years on, this is the most important missing result.
* **Labour cost per case, including overtime.**
* **CIs for sick days and resignations.** These are still raw comparisons between groups.

## Halden subset

* **High non-response.** Fourteen of 23 organisations responded, so 9 did not, and non-response is plausibly linked to how things went. Combined with the original attrition and self-selection, the 11 continuing organisations have been filtered three times, not two.
* **The hours baseline may not belong to this subset.** 40.3 is exactly the re-analysis's baseline for all 27 time-tracking organisations. The paper should confirm it is the 11-organisation figure and that all 11 have time-tracking data. Only 17 of the original 23 did.
* **Long-run trends.** Comparing month 24 with a baseline 2.5 years earlier picks up general productivity changes, such as new tools and changing workloads. "Upper bound" is a reasonable reading but not guaranteed, because these trends could push either way.
* **The marketing agency doesn't fit the summary.** The Summary says all reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations". The marketing agency cited client deadlines, which is not a coverage constraint, and marketing was in the discretionary group. That makes it the first reverting organisation outside the coverage-bound group, and it deserves mention rather than being grouped with the coverage cases.

## Smaller points

* **Counter-office costs.** Twelve percent more staff restores roughly the output lost (1/0.886 ≈ +13%), but at full pay that implies about +12% cost per contact, not +9%. The 9% figure presumably includes non-labour costs; the paper should say so.
* **Characterisation of the re-analysis.** It extrapolated energy returning to baseline around month ten and inferred that the per-hour gain was novelty. It did not literally predict "gain zero by month ten". The rebuttal still holds, but the paraphrase should be exact.
* **Authorship.** The original Halden author is a coauthor of this follow-up. That's fine, but a note on how the 14 organisations were contacted and whether the re-analysis team was offered the data would pre-empt questions about independence. A note on whether the Halden working paper was corrected for the misreported attrition would also help.

## Where the five documents leave things

| Question | Best current answer | Change since last round |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain (discretionary work) | About +8–10% at 24 months, CI excludes zero | Now from a controlled 2-year study with stricter hours measurement |
| Durability | Partly persists; some fading possible, but not established | Decline may partly reflect control offices cutting meetings |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Not supported | Strengthened |
| Meta-analysis "no decay" | Not supported; its long-run studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours | Settled |
| Coverage-bound work | Output and service fall; restoring them costs about 9–12% more per contact | Arm ended; costs now quantified |
| Mechanism | Meeting cuts are the leading candidate, fatigue secondary, about a third unexplained | Registered, but tested in the same offices that generated the hypothesis |
| Could reorganisation alone capture the gain? | Open; two control offices are suggestive | New question; needs a trial arm that reorganises without cutting hours |

The most useful next study would add that missing arm: offices that run a structured meeting audit and workflow reorganisation without cutting hours. That would directly test whether the hours cut is the cause or only the trigger.

I can draft that design or write a consolidated summary of all five documents.
